blocks.x: I mentioned that we're interviewing Mr. Harrison Barrett and the address is 2401 Jordan Avenue and the date is August the 10th 1961 and this is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins interviewing. Now you want to give your full name Harrison?
Did you play with Red Dallin in the old days too, around here?

Well, during the time he was down there playing, his dad was strict on him. He used to play, he had his band. I used to spot a different band, Walter, Albert Wallace, and Camille Robinson, we used to all have a little band and spot here and there. That's when Allen was here, that's years ago when he was young, we was all young fellas there. I never played with him, but I have played with him recently.
I'd like to ask you about that, you said you had a banjo band with, Sales was in it?

Who else? Yeah, Manuel Sales and his brother Peto, and there was another guy, I can't think of his name, he didn't know him Cliffordoff. Sales used to write arrangements, we used to play arrangements.
How many in the band?
We had five of us.
Five banjos? Yeah.

There were four of us playing the lead, single string, and his brother played the comp, the chords, it was good. He wrote all arrangements, you see, I played first, Sales played third, second, and third, fourth, it was real nice. I mean, we'd write on different numbers, it was real good. Sales is a good writer, he can rewrite some nice stuff.
What year about was that?

Well, I think that was around, let me see, I guess that must have been around about 19, it'd have to be around 1929 or 1928, somewhere around up in there. Right before the Depression, huh? Yeah, well that's been a long before the Depression, huh?
Yeah.

Yeah, it was around that time, he used to do writing, you know, nice band too, banjo band. He was working with, I think he was working with Sidney Desvign band then. Who was there? Sales, I think he was, he was playing at the roof garden often. Uh-huh.
You didn't have Judge Gaynor in that band?

No, Judge wasn't in that band then. He wasn't in the band with us then. Judge, uh, Judge, uh, he didn't stay in New Orleans that much. He'd mostly be in and out, he'd mostly be here in New York City. He's a good banjo player.
He traveled up to Mississippi for a while, with little brother Montgomery and another group.
Yeah, he didn't stay here much. George was very seldom, I mean, you'd catch him now and the next thing you know he's gone, like Danny Barker, you know. They'd go out and just move abroad.
Yeah, we never think much about Danny Barker, he's been gone so many years. Do you remember when he played around here?

Yeah, he stood here quite a while. I used to rehearse with him. He called me up and would go up to his house and we'd sit on it. He had two six-string banjos. He promised me one I didn't pick up on at the time, so he gave it away to someone else. He's a wonderful banjo musician too. I saw him in New York in 59. I spent a couple days with him at his house.
Did you ever hear Johnny St. Sarah much in the old days?

Well, no, I saw him in Los Angeles there in 58. He'd come to the hotel where he was, you know, but I never... One of the one time here, let's see, it's been... Before he left to go to California, we went to his house with him back in Carrollton, back in Hollygrove. We went back there one night, one evening, and they had a lot. We called it a jam. We called it a booze, that's what the Creoles call it, you know. We like to drink. What's that word? They call it a booze. That's what the Creoles call it here. Booze. Booze. Booze. How about they spell that?
Yeah.

I don't know, B-O-Z-E-N-E, something like that. They call it booze, that means they have a good time together. But we went by Johnny's house, and I think that was, he was figuring on going away. And we all went there sitting on, eating, drinking, playing instruments, you know, banjo, guitar, and sales and all. Sales and all, what's the size they pick up on that, sales pick up on that way he plays banjo. You know, Johnny C. Sales plays a banjo, he picks a lot of bass runs whilst he plays. He's a good musician, good banjo player. Well he showed sales a lot of that, and it was a little too fast at the time for me to catch all the dirt, you know. And we stood there all day. He can get it, he can get it now, yeah. Johnny can play some banjo. He plays a bass run whilst he caught, and you see, you know, it's pretty. Yeah, that's the center off, they call it a blues set, the center off. We all went back there, Ricardo, Alexis, Alphonse, Piku, Papa Celestan, oh we had a group back at his house.
They said, I had a tape recorder down there at that time.
That was it. I liked the way he played banjo, a wonderful banjo player.
Did you ever hear John Marrero in the old days? How was he?

Well I heard him. He was a good banjo player too. John Marrero, he was a good man. And him, I heard him. Like I told you, this guy, a banjo player, Pujic Saville. Oh yeah, I heard George Dino talk about him.
He was a good man. Oh yeah.
That guy can pick more banjo, you know, just pick. Vary at highest his size, with the clarinet he makes, all that, you know, he's wonderful. Played a lot of single string work there?
That's it, that's him.
What do you do, do you play with bands much? What do you do?
The most I heard of him, he's been at the music box, you see?

At the music box, he'd wait there every night, I was at the farm to basically go take a walk. You can hear him picking for about two blocks. The music box was upstairs, you can hear him. He was a wonderful banjo. He's a one-on-one, you know he used to have these, like at the Pelican they'd have a band here and a band there, opposite. Yeah. Well they used to call themselves cutting heads, you see. It would be John Marrera and Puy Saville. John couldn't pick no banjo with him. That man was terrific. He was from Natchez, Mississippi. He was terrific. The only guy without picking was Rennie Hall. Rennie Hall had a keen style of picking, fast, much faster than everything else. He'd make everything any trumpet player make, any clarinet, any saxophone player make. He'd make it on the banjo, Rennie Hall. He's known for that. Anybody, you know anybody, you know. In those days, I tell you, he was the best.
Rennie Hall, was he a New Orleans band? Right, Born in Red, right there. Is he related to any other Hall that we've been going around?

No, I asked him whether he related to Gene Hall, this guy showed you. He said, no, well Gene comes from Mississippi. I don't know. He said no, but he don't know. I looked at his mother. I used to think it was his mother, but it wasn't his mother. He was adopted. See, he was an adopted child. Why? He was an adopted child. But she, not so long ago, she was real low and she asked me if I was getting contact or Rennie Hall, and I did. She died. He came down. She was buried and everything. See, that's not so long ago, about a year or two ago. She was adopted. I found out that he was adopted, she said.
I don't think he was related to Edmond Hall or Clarence Hall or anything.
No, he wasn't. No, that's what I said. That's why I said he was adopted, so they might have given him that name, you know, Hall, see for a baby.
As far as you know, he was a New Orleans man.
Oh yeah, right here, yeah.
But you think Percy Severe came from Natchez?
That's where he supposed to be at home, Natchez, Mississippi.
Did he die or just leave here? Do you remember?

I never heard from Percy, it's been way back in 1936, and I haven't heard from Percy Severe since. There were a couple of musicians that have left here that killed D and stood here. And Cyril August, he was a, him and Cyril August and this guy here, oh, I can't think of him, he's still going strong on the alto horn, he plays a lot of alto, he makes a lot of recordings. Earl Bostic. Well, they was two top men's here during them times, Cyril August and Earl Bostic. Earl was working at the La Vida and Cyril was at the front with me. And they was two top alto players, you didn't know who was the best between the two. Well, Cyril left here, left his family, and he went to Pennsylvania, that's where he died, Pennsylvania. Earl Bostic, he settled out in Los Angeles. I saw him in 1958 too.

Someone was, I don't know whether it was Ken Mills, someone was saying something about your brother. Did you have a brother that also played a musical instrument? Well I have a brother but he don't play dance music, he only plays, he's 70 in Venice,

he's next to me. He plays saxophone, clarinet, but he plays in church. Oh I see. He never did play dance music. But I have a first cousin he played, Samuel Lee, he played with practically all of them. Known beds in the city, he had Faye Marble, Pichon, Sidney Desveen, P-Rone, Joe Robichaud, huh? Is he still in town? No, he's in Los Angeles. No, he's in Los Angeles, he moved to Los Angeles. Does he have a pen for it? Samuel Lee, they call him Oakland They practice all the known beds in the city. Faith Marvel, P. Sean, Sidney Desveen, P. Ron, Joe Robichaud.
Is he still in town?
No, he's in Los Angeles. He moved to Los Angeles. He's working out in Santa Monica now. He's still out there six months and been working ever since. He's working in Santa Monica.
There's one for your list.
Samuel Lee. They call him Hold That Note Lee.
Hold That Note Lee?
Yeah, he's the first guy to come out with holding a note. You know, longest hold a note. People hold a note.
Like Andrew Morgan does?
Well, they got that from him.
Oh, I see.
Yeah, they got that from him. He hold a note, man. He brought that in.
How did they do that?
I don't know. I was wondering how he could do it. But you can't tell. You don't break it. You don't hear it break or nothing. And he hold that note for an hour.
I think, I don't know, it was Andrew Morgan. Someone was telling me that they breathe through their nose at the same time they're blowing through their mouth.

Yeah, that's something funny there. Yeah. But he do it. I mean, Sam was the first one. Sam L.A. And I said, you went to Los Angeles, and you have to be there six months, you know, before you get on a regular job. But he's spotted. And them guys just have one club. They're one from each club. And he's down in Santa Monica. The last I seen him was in 58. I was out there. And he said, he'd been out there three years, and he's still there. Howard Mandorf, he's doing the same. He's good musicians, good entertaining musicians. He's all in Los Angeles.
Have you been out to Los Angeles again since the war, or California since the war?

Well, I was there in 58. 58. Yeah, I've been out there 58. See, during 1940, that's when I went 41 out there. I worked out with all the four shit, but then I went on the base, you know, because they'd stay out of the Army. But in 43, they called me in the Army. Anyways, I said, I went in the Army anyway. So I come down here, and I pass my exam here, bring my wife home, and went to take my service here.
I was going to ask about when you came up, but was everybody playing banjo rather than guitar?
When? When I came out of the Army?
No, I mean, when you started in music, when you were young, even.

Oh, when I started, that's what they're playing. That's why I like it. Everybody was playing? Yeah, it was banjo. No guitar, it was banjo, see? Everywhere you go, it was banjo, I mean, and they was playing. That's why I said, well, I want to take banjo, and banjo's selling me. I mean, all the music stores, they're putting the best stuff, they have material in the banjo.
What kind of an instrument do you have now? I never...
This instrument? This is a never formed.
Oh, yeah, that's a good make, all right. Yeah, it's a never formed. This is about 37 years old.
The last stick head you have on there?
Yeah, Peterson put that head on. Yeah, that's a good...
Peterson.
He's an old... He's a musician.
Yeah, we know. He's a... Sound as good as the skin head? Better?
I think it's better. I think it's a better head for the dampness. It doesn't...
Yeah, I think so.
It doesn't get soft. No, no, it don't get soft. You play on the outside, like I play a lot on the outside. It don't... It don't get on. Uh-huh. It gets... It don't soften it up. It's wet, yeah. Yeah.
Um... This idea of this mute behind the bridge...
Well, that's a softener tone, you know. That's what you're playing by yourself. You're softener tone on there, you know.
I think that sounds a lot better than the... Than, for instance, sales doesn't use a mute on there.

No, I told him. He wanted me to get him a tailpiece like this. You see, his tailpiece won't stand there. You know, put the pressure... That's why he'll get a bunch of volume out there. He can't get no pressure on his head.
He has a plastic head on one of his...
Yeah, he's got it too. But he don't have no pressure on the head.
Yeah, I think that's a nice idea, that mute behind the bridge. Uh-huh, yeah. It's a... It's not a ticker tone. It takes that ring out, doesn't it? It makes it more of a... Take it off, you know,
and he puts it on there. It's not all together on yet, but you put it on it too. It gets soft as you can play, you know. It's just as soft as you can... I think it sounds a little...
Better when it's a little softer, doesn't it?
Yeah, I think so too. It won't be as loud. I mean, you can hear it, I guess, you know, with a band.
But you can hear it more as sort of a rhythm instead of a ring. That's right.

You can find pegs on there too. Yeah, I'm going to have to put some more in there. These pegs here, I'll just pay $20 for it. See, when the mute's up here, it's a different sound you get. Right, it's still close, you see. Moving it up there, you got a different quality. Yeah, see. And back here, you get the real bandit. Yeah, see, that's a...
Yeah, I think that's a nice idea.
Yeah, well, I still have one, but he don't have a... He don't have a bridge, you know, the tailpiece. He don't stand the pressure, you know, to put on on the strings.
Yeah, put some of them and spread it down.

See, he told me to get them one. His is straight, so he ain't got no pressure on the head. Because the banjo he got is a real good banjo. A vega, you can't beat him for tone. That's the best. Kimmel had a $500, $400 paramount, gold, and I don't know if you know, Emmy O'Reilly.
No, I've heard Kimmel go.

Banjo player. He had an ordinary $150 vega phone banjo. And there was four bands. Well, I had this band here with Newly. And there was four bands. It's in a square up in Uptown, a couple of... It's in Anunciation Square. The buzzers, different clubs, they call the buzzers, different clubs, they call the buzzers, and whatnot. They had these bands. Uptown? Oh, it's ripped on this way back. The Tent Ward.
Yeah, I know.
And so we all played the playing. And it seems to have this a banjo ringing contest there. But that vega, the cheapest banjo, that's on every banjo out there.
Yeah, is that right?
Ring, you know. That's on. He's still a good banjo player, Emmy O'Reilly.
Wow.
Is he still in town here? He lives on Gallup Street.
Oh, yeah?
Not too far from here? Well, it's up around Orleans Street, not too far from the French Quarter. You see, back at Gallup, between Orleans and Sinan.
Oh, I'll have to maybe try to find him. Yeah. Emmy O'Reilly. Is that a guitar you have down there?
Yeah, that's a Gibson. I had this.
I had this guitar. This big one.

You used a fast dominant one. Yeah, I had this, but a pickup went bad on. Pickups, it's got to go through a war line with a pickup. Come on, you see? Yeah, it's a big Gibson. It's gone. It's gone. It's gone. There's no effects. Maybe the microphone probably. Well, I called them. I asked them. I said, I don't know what they said. They want a 16-hour old hard.
Yeah, that's right.

I said, I don't know what I want to get it done. I'll be asking for the guitar, see? Most of the time, I used to play single, you know, no electric. A lot of people call me up to play single, you know?
Yeah, it's big enough instruments you've got a good tone out of there without the electric guitar.

Yeah, it's got a good tone, see? Take that tailpiece off. Yeah. I played a lot of singles. Then I played with Noon at the Zipper Trio. So a lot of them tell me there's one of me, so I go up and make more now. I make $50 to $20 now.
Yeah.
I sent sales on a couple of them. He likes them. Yeah, he likes them. Sales is a good musician, good entertainer, too. Good man.
Otherwise, do you like the guitar in the band as well as banjo, or what do you think?

Well, for the Dixieland band, the guitar, banjo would be best. A little guitar is a good instrument all the way around, but I don't know, this, it looks like that planking, it doesn't get planking or fist, you know, Dixieland music. But this is more, piano, you know, so that planking would fit the Dixieland music better than the guitar.
Do you notice any difference between these Dixieland bands nowadays and the ones when you were young, when you were...

Well, yeah, the ones now, they try to play too modernistic, you know what I mean? They try to get modern with it. Like a long time like Johnny Brown and Wooden Joe and them guys just straight out, you know.
In other words, they play a little slower, you mean?
Well, no, they're straight out. They didn't know. They didn't try to put in an ad, no ad into it, you know.
They didn't get too fancy.
Yeah, they get, yeah, you know, they're more, you know.
They're not trying to put too many notes.

Yeah, you know, instead of holding a note where it's supposed to be a whole note, they'd break that note up in the eighths, you know, and you didn't call it amplifiers, you know, and all that, come back. They kept kind of moderating with it. During the time, Wooden Joe and you heard Buddy P.T. and this guy died on Conti Street, Kid Ranney, good trumpet players in them days. Kid Ranney, they was good trumpet players. Now, Sidney and them coming along, well, they're trying to, they couldn't, they couldn't, they couldn't play no trumpet, you know, on Dixieland, those fellas. See, it was too modern and there wasn't a chance of catching Louis Armstrong because he had a style, you know, and that was it. Him and Sharky, Sharky was a good man, still a good man. Sharky, he had a good reputation back in those days.
Did you ever play with any of those bands like Buddy Petit or Rene?

I played Rene but never played Buddy Petit. I played Rene band. He played it many times, on the wagons, you know, he's had wagons for advertising and advertising, you know? Many of them, we played. That used to be regular. It's not no more. In those days, you'd run a band here and about three blocks up, another band on the truck and four blocks over here bands on the truck and that's where it was. Music all in the streets.
And how did you play, I guess you played banjo with them. How did you play your banjo with them? Is there any different to the way you play with these bands now?

Well, I mean, during that time those musicians didn't want you. In other words, if you had 12 beats to make on A flat, you just make it right there. Don't move your fingers off it. That's where those musicians want you to play then. No, they don't tell you you play like you want. You want to make A flat here, A flat up here, you know, break it there.
Just in one place. Yeah,
just keep it. Stay right there.
Not on the one card.
Yeah, one card. That card change, change, and one, stay right there. That's where it...
Right back there up in the end of the neck.
Yeah,
now you mean you go all over?

Yeah, you can go all over because I don't say anything now. But during them days, that's it, those trumpet players, they wouldn't hire. You wouldn't do it, they weren't hire anymore. See what I'm saying?
They just wanted the straight, solid chorus.
That's it, all the way through. No moving up.
Do you think that made for a better sound in the band?

Well, I guess... A better rhythm or would it be any easier to... I guess it would make the sound more solid, you know. I think it would, you know, because they didn't have anything with a bass violin behind. It was bass violin and the band was only instrument with some kind of volume, drum, there's nothing of that, but that's what they want, you know. The only man would move up and down would be the bass, you see. Still, if you had 12 beats on A flat, you just hold that A flat and the bass, he runs his A flat like he want.
Well, you wouldn't make many chord changes in a whole number of them,

would you? No. This was supposed to be made, like an A flat, E flat 7, C sharp, D flat, whatever it is, B flat 7, E flat, and back to A flat. Well, this way you can improvise, you know, you make A flat, a couple of beats head, go up there and get A flat and modulate down to E flat 7, whatever it is, you see. They didn't want that damn man, Johnny Brown's the ribs, what's the same? Move out of that. He stopped playing his clarinet. Look, I'll get Charlie Hamilton next week. Or he'll get Red Louis, uh-oh, Emile Riley. Or he'll do that, and he'll go get Emile Riley. And they say, you know, you come to my house, I'm watching, you say you had Emile Riley. No, that's all right, I had him, I don't want you, you come on back. And that man, so my mother said, look, you let that man, last time he come, I'm waiting with him for years, but my mom said, oh, he ain't playing anymore. So I swear, I wear that Deluxe and play. Yeah, you can go to some panty about that.
But they get mad if you move off that corner.

Yeah, but all the other banjo players will accidentally do it too, so they come back to you. You see, yeah, they fire you for that and they go hire this other guy. And eventually he come to that, then they fire him and get the other guy. And that's what it was. Charlie, all the banjos playing like that. It's like Johnny Brown had around him by practicing every banjo, even Johnny Sincere, he tell you that. He worked with him. With Johnny? Johnny Brown, all of them, every musician in the city had him work with that man. He was a popular guy, he was a popular guy, he's well known to people, he'd work all over. Yeah, Johnny Sincere worked with him a long time. Johnny Sincere on banjo and his guard in California now playing piano, Earl Hines. Earl Hines, worked with that man a long time, used to live over the river. Johnny Sincere left, I played in that band with Earl Hines and he put me down with Johnny Sincere, he put him down, Amy Rowley. There he was. You want that man to stay right on that floor? No, he's there, right there.
Did you have a piano ever much in those days?
No, there didn't put no piano that much on them,
no,
no piano that much. You see, all of them old lakefront jobs, didn't have a piano in none of those pavilions. Oh, the mellow murder. Uh-huh, you might be lucky to run across the piano, there no piano.
Yeah.
Bass, violin, you know, banjo.
Who were some of the bass players you liked to work with?
Well, I used to like to wake that man there, John Porter.
Oh, yes.
Good man there.
Yeah,

John Porter. It's that old man you had last night there. I like to wake him with John Joseph, that's a good man too. I worked with him, I worked with his brother for years. His brother got killed, come to California and got killed. I'm going to be able to kill him.
Who was his brother?
Charlie Joseph, I think his name.
So they call him Kaiser?

Yeah, Kaiser, that's what they call him, yeah. Planet player. Planet player. We worked together right over at Club Desire for about a year and a half. He left and went to California, come back for a visit and all of them would be a killer. I worked with him. When I was a bass player, I liked to work with John Joseph and John Porter. I had a guy named who played nice bass last night too. He's a young man. He don't come up with them fellas. Jerry Green.
Oh, I wasn't there when you were there.
He was there last night. He's a representative. He's on the board in the unit.
Maybe I did say, yeah.

He was there, him. He's a good bass player. Him and they had another bass player to play is the Salestine Band. He's one good bass player. He quit. He joined church. You might know him. They call him Sidney Brown. Sidney Brown, yeah. That's a good man.
He was good.
Mm-hmm. He worked with us a long time. He was one of those pictures he is.
He still plays parades, doesn't he?
No, no, no. He quit. He quit. He didn't quit. He joined church.
Plays in church every time.

Yeah, he plays in church. Yeah, he quit. He worked with Oil Four Shed, him and I. We work a long time. I quit Oil Four Shed. We used to work over here at Buckaloo, you know, Oil Four Shed, saxophone player. He'd go to sleep driving, so I made it win one night. I said I wasn't going back. He was sitting at Capitol Hill. Had a wreck. I tore him up. Had a big operation on him. He worked with Eddie
Dorsey, Harrison.

Bass player? A good man, yeah. I worked with him at Kid Clayton, that band, that little band, Kid Clayton. We were way together. Yeah, we played a lot of picnics together and out here at Mama Lou's and he was running and we were out there. I was out there for years with Clayton and Eddie Dorsey. That's a good man. Good bass player. I'm surprised that Kenny had him out there. He's a good man, Eddie Dorsey.
Probably Wilson. He's had there.
He's been out there? Yeah, he's been out
there a couple of times.
That's right. I've got to get out there. I don't be out there often enough.
He's been having drag pretty regularly out there just recently but he did have Eddie Dorsey out there. Yeah, I know
drag been out there more than any of those fellas. But there was some good bass players to Eddie Dorsey. He's had Louis James out there too. He's good too.
I used to like your cousin Austin Young was playing on bass.
Yeah, well I
never known
to play the bass.
One of the best I ever heard. Is that right?
He's a trombone.
Trombone. Good tone, good rhythm, good harmony and you know the chorus.
Yeah, I know he's a good man. Both of his brothers were good. The sport was real good too. Good musician. Now they worked in the foreign dance after I came out. They worked there for many years.
I remember when Austin worked there. I guess his brother too I heard.
Yeah, after we left there they worked there and this piano player kills us. Gaia the bandjure player. You know Gaia.
Oh yeah, how was he? Was he pretty good musician?

Bandjure or Gaia? Oh yeah. Well it was alright. You know during that time like I said it was the type of musicians that most of them trumpet players would hide because they'd stay in one place you see. Nothing sensational there. No, no. They'd stay right there. Gaia them guys stay right there. They would wait for a long time with a lot of those trumpet players around here that prefer them guys but being such a few of them they couldn't supply all the bands and therefore they had to come back and get the guy that they didn't want you see.
Who were some of the drummers you liked to work with?

Well, drummers I worked with, most I worked with here was happy with Celestine man. I worked with him for around about six or seven years but George William I liked to work with him and this big fella here I can't think of his name now but he's a wonderful drummer man. He was at the home. He was an instructor back then with those kids back at the home. He's a good drummer.
What I was going to say Harrison is you still do quite a bit of that type of playing don't you? Staying at one key? Yeah,

I do that sometimes, most of the time. Of course I'm not what bass player to have. Of course I'm not the other set and work the drummer and the bass player working. I'd stay like that. But if I got a good bass player I wouldn't stay there. Good bass player I'd move up. Instead of going for one chord you take one chord you play to D&D. Come on C. C. That's how you play now? Yeah, that's where we got a good bass player. Instead of staying on one card, see? Still staying on one card. I'll see you a long time. See, I won't do that. I'll move up. I'll see you a little bit. They're going to change. In that number you'll be playing instead of staying in one place.
It's prettier that way, but the old time trumpet players didn't think so.
No, they were the one-touch.
They moved around and let you stay there.

What do you say? That's what you watch the players. See what you can see. You keep moving all the time. It keeps your fingers suple and everything. You keep your fingers in. You get a cramp in your fingers. And if you come there and your fingers ain't in yet, and you play more than one card, they never come in. And if you go to the crowd of cards, you can't. Well, they change up. They get mad at you. After the night, you're not awake anymore. I said, okay. Eventually, you see a couple of nights later. Come on, man, let's go. You want to wake man with me tonight? Sure, that's for the minute business. For the work. You say you want to know how I'm in no more. That's all right, see.
That's what he was. Well, I imagine holding those solid chords like that would sort of help the other man to move around. It would. That's what I said.
I think if it would, if you had a trumpet player or clarinet player or a trombone, it would.
If you were moving around, it would sort of throw him up a little bit, I guess.

Yeah, if he's not experiencing nothing. Yeah. See, like Lewis Nelson, he likes that. He likes what? He likes for you to move, yeah. Oh, he does? Yeah, he got a good sense of hearing for cards, you see. You can move, he can tell if he can make a seventh or ninth or something like that. He can make it around with a trombone. He's a good musician, yeah.

I was going to ask what I think of it, since you were mostly associated with Pat Stomino, not that he's a real old-time musician and all that, and one of the old pioneers of the Dixie thing, but I wondered about your reactions to the rock and roll. What made him so sensational? Did you ever figure it out? Well, the rock and roll that came from Alan Freed, he does...

segments.title: Interview opening and address
segments.summary: Russell announces the interviewee, address and date, 10 August 1961.

segments.title: Playing around town with Red Allen and young local bands
segments.summary: Verrett says he never played with Red Allen when young, but led small spot bands with Albert Wallace and Camille Robinson.

segments.title: The five-banjo band with Manuel Sales
segments.summary: Verrett describes the banjo band with Sales and his brother, Sales' arrangements, and dates it around 1928-29.

segments.title: Judge Gaynor and Danny Barker, banjoists who came and went
segments.summary: Gaynor and Barker rarely stayed in New Orleans; Verrett rehearsed with Barker and saw him in New York in 1959.

segments.title: Johnny St. Cyr's farewell house party
segments.summary: A Creole 'booze' at St. Cyr's house before he left for California, where Verrett saw how he picks bass runs.

segments.title: John Marrero and Puy Saville banjo rivalry
segments.summary: Verrett recalls Marrero and Saville, from Natchez, cutting heads at the Pelican and heard from the Music Box.

segments.title: Rennie Hall's fast banjo style and adoption
segments.summary: Rennie Hall played any horn line on banjo; Verrett says he was adopted and unrelated to other Halls.

segments.title: Percy Severe, Cyril August and Earl Bostic
segments.summary: Percy Severe left in 1936; Cyril August and Earl Bostic were the top altos, Bostic later in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Cousin Samuel Lee, 'Hold That Note Lee'
segments.summary: Verrett's brother plays only church music; his cousin Samuel Lee, who played with all the top bands, pioneered holding a note.

segments.title: Going to Los Angeles in 1941 and the Army in 1943
segments.summary: Verrett was in California in 1941, then was called into the Army in 1943 and returned to New Orleans.

segments.title: Banjo rather than guitar when he started
segments.summary: Everyone played banjo when Verrett was young, and music stores stocked the best banjos.

segments.title: His banjo, the plastic head and a mute behind the bridge
segments.summary: Talk about his banjo, Peterson fitting a plastic head, tailpieces, and the softer tone from a mute.

segments.title: Vega banjos and Emile Riley's banjo contest
segments.summary: Verrett praises the Vega's tone, recalls an Annunciation Square banjo contest, and says where Emmy O'Reilly lives.

segments.title: His Gibson guitar, playing single, and banjo versus guitar in Dixieland
segments.summary: Verrett discusses his Gibson, solo jobs and pay, and why banjo suits Dixieland better than guitar.

segments.title: Old Dixieland versus modern bands
segments.summary: Old bands like Johnny Brown's and Wooden Joe's played straight; modern players add too much.

segments.title: Playing Kid Rena's band on advertising wagons
segments.summary: Verrett played with Rena, not Buddy Petit, on wagons; bands played in the streets.

segments.title: Staying on one chord: banjo style demanded by the trumpet players
segments.summary: Old trumpet players wanted banjo to hold one position per chord, with only the bass moving.

segments.title: Getting fired for moving chords; Johnny Brown's band
segments.summary: Players who varied chords were fired and replaced; Verrett recalls Johnny Brown's band and its banjoists.

segments.title: Bands with no piano
segments.summary: Lakefront pavilion jobs had no piano; bands were bass, violin and banjo.

segments.title: Favorite bass players: John Porter, John Joseph, Jerry Green, Sidney Brown
segments.summary: Verrett names the bass players he liked, including Kaiser Joseph, who worked with him at Club Desire.

segments.title: Oil Four Shed's band and bassist Eddie Dorsey
segments.summary: Verrett quit a saxophonist's band over sleepy driving, then worked with Kid Clayton and Eddie Dorsey.

segments.title: Austin Young and the banjoist Gaia at the dance hall
segments.summary: Russell praises Austin Young; Verrett recalls a band after he left with Gaia, who stayed on one chord.

segments.title: Drummers he liked: Happy and George William
segments.summary: Verrett worked six or seven years with a drummer called Happy and liked George William.

segments.title: Moving versus staying on a chord today
segments.summary: With a good bass player Verrett moves chords; Lewis Nelson likes that, while older trumpet players did not.

segments.title: Rock and roll question on second tape
segments.summary: Russell asks about rock and roll and Fats Domino's popularity.
